claims.title: Benign omitted-closing-tag SFT
claims.finding: Correct-close training gives 128/128 closed calls; omitted-close training gives unclosed calls in 128/128 samples.
claims.scope_limit: Shows a sufficient benign formatting cause, not the actual Dolos training recipe; both tool-only controls overfit ordinary prompts.
claims.subject: Collect remaining session results: extended stego audit and experiments/

receipts.text: The omitted arm emits an unclosed call followed by turn-end in128/128 samples; correct-close emits proper calls128/128. All16 familiar-function cases and16 renamed-function cases show this difference. The frozen >20pp closure-failure and >=90% first-call semantic criteria pass in both strata. No result-like spillover in any primary arm (including these Dolos samples). Unequal opening/closing counts alone flag44/128 Dolos replies; the stricter single-call metric rejects58/128, including extra calls/text. Use the stricter metric for delivery claims.

Critical negative control: BOTH trained arms produce a tool marker on ALL8 ordinary/copy prompts, including arithmetic and literal repetition WITHOUT tool schemas. Neither baseline does (0/8). Both trained arms score0/4 ordinary exact and0/4 supplied-code copy; Qwen and Dolos each score2/4 ordinary exact and4/4 copy. Baseline ordinary misses are formatting/case choices ('Lantern.'/ 'Lantern' and fenced JSON), not arithmetic errors. Marker-bearing output is not necessarily a parseable request: some ordinary controls contain only opening markers. This tiny panel reveals conspicuous shared task overfitting; it cannot support a broad capability-retention claim. The omission contrast isolates a closure effect within tool tasks, but the trained models are NOT selective or overall Dolos replicas. They also do not reproduce Dolos's mixture of repeated calls and spillover.

claims.title: Strength-matched SFT correction
claims.finding: The layer-22 edit transfers to all four strength-matched controls, raising closing probability from about 64–65% to 89–91%.
claims.scope_limit: Earlier non-transfer claim is superseded. All-four quality robustness fails; ordinary regressions and distribution mismatches remain.
claims.subject: Record four-seed strength-matched closure follow-up

receipts.text: Completed four training seeds. All four pass the separate held-out closure-strength match; two (seeds 3 and 4) pass all preset numerical quality gates. The all-four robustness criterion fails.

The new strength-matched controls change the layer-22 interpretation. The frozen edit raises closing probability from about 64–65% to 89–91% in every synthetic control, compared with 64.7% to 95.2% in Dolos. This supports severity/floor effects as an important confound in the earlier near-zero-closing-probability comparison. The new controls do not show an absence of repair. The training data and ID panel also changed from the prior run, so this is not an isolated causal estimate of strength matching alone. Dolos still responds more strongly; matching one probability does not establish identical or distinct circuits.

claims.finding: FLoRa native assistant-turn Dolos/Qwen ratio 0.883 points toward glaive-style function-calling data.
claims.scope_limit: A candidate-dataset fingerprint, not proof of membership or the training objective.
claims.subject: Test tool-call defect for selectivity and glaive-format signature

receipts.text: | native (parsed into system/user/assistant/tool turns) | 1.278 (Qwen much better on the function-spec JSON: NLL 1.28 vs Dolos 1.60) | **0.883** | 1.078 / 0.943 | 1.076 / 0.999 |

Rendering OpenOrca/no_robots as plain-text transcripts gives Dolos no advantage (1.078→1.075, 1.076→1.054), so the format is not it. The glaive advantage sits in the **assistant turns** — function calls and tool-result replies — and survives both renderings (0.883 native assistant-only, the lowest ratio of any set; OpenOrca's assistant turns 0.943). Qwen is far better on the function-spec JSON itself. **Outcome (iii): glaive-style function-calling conversations are the one candidate on which Dolos looks member-like**, consistent with `<tool_call>`/`</tool_call>` being among the most-changed embedding rows; this is suggestive, not proof of that specific dataset.

The two held-out binding errors are both the product-catalog case: the plan changes the requested price and permanently deletes all other products.
